Each merge is a learned rule joining two neighbours. Repeat until the list holds 32,000 entries.","headline":{"text":"Learn pieces by merging pairs","semantic":"concept"},"tags":["merge loop","frequent pair"],"statCards":[{"value":"32,000","label":"vocabulary entries","sourceRef":"num-1"}],"source":"A field guide to subword merges"},{"beatId":"b5","narration":"Encoding new text replays those merges in order. An unusual word stays in pieces, because no merge ever joined it.","headline":{"text":"'the' = one token","semantic":"concept"},"tags":["one token","stays in pieces"]},{"beatId":"b6","narration":"So why three times? Because merges were learned from mostly English text. The translated reply has few merges of its own, so it stays in small pieces, the same meaning, about 3 times as many tokens.","headline":{"text":"Few merges, three times the tokens","semantic":"problem"},"tags":["few merges","small pieces"],"statCards":[{"value":"about 3","label":"times the tokens of English","sourceRef":"num-6"}],"source":"Field notes: counting tokens before you pay for them"},{"beatId":"b7","narration":"And small details change the split. A space stays with the word after it, and digits split one at a time. So the same name can be one token or three, depending on capitals.","headline":{"text":"Same name, one token or three","semantic":"problem"},"tags":["case matters","digits split"],"statCards":[{"value":"three","label":"tokens for all-caps name","sourceRef":"num-7"}],"source":"glyphcut"},{"beatId":"b8","narration":"So Corrowby counted with the exact tokenizer and wrote budgets in tokens.
